Robert McGrue organized a party of 20 to travel from Salt Lake City to the San Juan Mountains after hearing of gold discovered in Breckenridge.
The party left in November 1873.
George Tracy said the party encountered a 23-year-old man called Alfred Packer near Provo.
Packer said he wanted to join the party, claiming he was both a prospector and a guide who knew the San Juan territory well.
Packer offered $25 to join the band because he had no provisions.
The prospectors accepted Packer’s help because they needed a guide.
Party members later said Packer may have overstated or fabricated his familiarity with the area.
Packer was reported to have left with only a Colt revolver and no rifle.
During the journey, Packer was reported to be greedy with rations, lazy, obstinate, and obsessed with the amount of money the party carried.
Packer quarreled constantly with Frank Miller.
Preston Nutter later called Packer a “whining fraud” at Packer’s first trial.
Packer’s epileptic seizures made his presence in the group strenuous.
There were rumors that Packer had spent time in jail in Salt Lake City on a charge of murdering a hunting partner.
The party progressed more slowly than expected toward Breckenridge despite Packer serving as guide.
Winter crippled wagons and horses and the party was slowed by heavy snow along the Spanish Trail.
The party relied almost solely on a compass after heavy snow hid the path.
Packer’s inexperience showed itself and the party became lost.
Provisions ran out and the men first survived on horse feed.
The men neared the point of eating the horses themselves.
On January 21, 1874, the party reached Chief Ouray’s camp near Montrose, Colorado, in the Uncompahgre Valley.
Chief Ouray was known as the White Man’s Friend.
Chief Ouray supplied the party with food and lodging.
Chief Ouray recommended that the party postpone the expedition until spring because winter weather in the mountains was dangerous.
Chief Ouray told them no Ute would attempt such a journey and that trying it meant risking almost certain death.
Chief Ouray offered to let the men stay with his tribe until winter had passed.
Chief Ouray promised to share all that he and his people had with the men.
Despite the warnings, 11 men decided to continue on.
The men intended to travel first to the Los Pinós Indian Agency and then proceed to Breckenridge.
Chief Ouray provided food for the journey and safe directions to bypass the mountains.
Packer wanted to reach the agency by going through the mountains because he said it was a more direct route.
The party split into two groups, with five men following Oliver Loutsenhizer along the Gunnison River and six others, including Packer, heading through the San Juan Mountains.
Loutsenhizer threatened to shoot Packer if Packer wanted to follow the other group.
On February 9, Packer and five others left for the Los Pinós Indian Agency, 75 miles ahead.
Bob McGrue guided Packer’s men along the river route advised by Chief Ouray until the horses could not continue.
McGrue unloaded the men’s provisions and went back to Ouray’s camp.
Packer then took his party higher into the San Juan Mountains against Ouray’s warning.

The men entered the mountains with barely enough food for the supposed 14 days of the safest route, no snowshoes, minimal matches, no flint, no heavy clothing, two rifles, one pistol, a couple of knives, a hatchet, and minimal ammunition.
On April 16, 1874, 65 days after leaving, Packer emerged alone and crossed a frozen lake bed to the Los Pinós Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado.
Packer came to the agency during breakfast and begged for food and shelter.
Packer carried a rifle, a knife, a steel coffee pot, and a satchel.
Packer vomited when given food and said his digestion had changed because of prolonged near-starvation.
Packer told the agency that he had been hired by five men to guide them to Breckenridge.
Packer said he became snow-blind during the journey and was left behind as a burden.
Packer claimed Israel Swan gave him a rifle before the others abandoned him.
Packer said he survived alone on roots and rose buds and ate his moccasins.
The agency men thought Packer’s condition was odd because he did not look as malnourished and threadbare as expected after more than two months in the wilderness.
Packer’s face was reported as bloated and his physique was hardly skeletal.
Packer said he would drink whisky for breakfast instead of food.
Packer said he was broke and sold his Winchester rifle to Major Downer for $10.
Packer stayed at the agency for ten days and then went to Saguache to buy supplies for a trip back to Pennsylvania.
In Saguache, Packer bought a horse for $70 and booked a room at Dolan’s Saloon.
Larry Dolan later said Packer spent around $100 during his stay and offered to lend him $300.
Packer also spent $78 in Otto Mears’ general store.
It was claimed that Packer had several different wallets in his possession.
Preston Nutter arrived in Saguache with two other original party members and found Packer at Dolan’s Saloon.
When Nutter asked where the rest of the party was, Packer said he had gotten his feet wet and frozen.
Packer said the party camped when a winter storm started, that he made a fire while the others went ahead to find food, and that Swan left him with his rifle.
Packer said the others never returned and that he then made his way through the mountains eating mostly rosebuds and small animals.
Nutter found Packer’s story odd because Packer looked well-fed and because abandoning a guide in snowbound mountains seemed unlikely.
Nutter also thought it was strange that Swan would give Packer his rifle and leave four men with only one rifle for hunting.
Packer claimed Miller had stuck the knife in a tree and walked off without it.
Nutter said Packer was sulky, obstinate, quarrelsome, and a petty thief.
Two of the five men who had taken the Gunnison River route eventually arrived at the Los Pinós Indian Agency.
The remaining three men, including Loutsenhizer, arrived a few days later.
General Charles Adams told the men he had already met Alfred Packer and that Packer spoke of being deserted by his companions.
All five men immediately discredited Packer’s account to Adams and his staff.
Loutsenhizer said the Winchester rifle Packer carried belonged to an elderly man in the party.
Loutsenhizer said the pipe Packer left at the agency belonged to Shannon Bell.
The men persuaded Adams to send a mounted agency officer to Saguache to retrieve Packer for questioning while pretending to recruit him for a search party.
Packer was preparing to leave when Nutter and other men approached him again.
The agency officer arrived in time to separate the men.
The officer told Packer he had been sent to enlist him as a guide for the search party.
Packer agreed to return to Los Pinós because he had little alternative besides vigilante justice.
At the agency, Packer met General Adams and five men he had not seen since February.
Loutsenhizer demanded an explanation and Packer repeated his earlier story.
Packer acted amazed that the men had not been heard from and said he was concerned for their well-being.
When asked where his money came from, Packer said he had received a cash loan from a man in Saguache.
The officer also reported that Packer had arrived in Saguache with plenty of cash and that no one in town claimed to have lent him any money.
Adams convened a council of himself, Packer, and the agency officers.
Two Ute tribesmen then arrived with strips of dried human flesh they had found on a hill near the agency while hunting.
Packer begged for mercy and promised a full confession.
Herman Lauter transcribed Packer’s first official statement.
Packer said the men left Ouray’s camp with what they thought was enough food for a 14-day journey.
Packer said provisions ran out sooner than expected.
Packer said that after a few days of no wildlife and almost no food, the men began to eye each other unsettlingly.
Packer said he returned from gathering firewood to find four men around Israel Swan’s body after Swan had been struck in the head with a hatchet and killed instantly.
Packer said the four men butchered Swan and that he accepted the situation and joined them.
Packer said several thousand dollars was found on Swan and divided among the men.
Packer said they ate the best parts of Swan, packed some away, and continued onward with Packer taking Swan’s rifle.
Packer said the five men again ran out of meat within two days and could not find game.
Packer said Bell, Humphrey, Noon, and he secretly decided that Miller would be next because he was stocky and had soft flesh.
Packer said Miller was killed with a hatchet blow to the head while stooping to pick up firewood and was then butchered and eaten.
Packer said Humphrey was next to be sacrificed, followed soon after by George Noon.
Packer said only Bell and he were left and that they swore not to eat each other.
Packer said they agreed to claim the four other men had died from the elements and were buried with dignity.
Packer said they vowed never to speak of the cannibalism because they believed no one would accept that it had been necessary.
Packer said that after a few days of travel with only a rabbit and some roots to eat, he and Bell camped beside a large lake next to a grove of hemlock trees.
Packer said Bell later jumped from his blanket, screamed that he could not take it anymore, and said one of them would die for food.
Packer said Bell rushed at him with a rifle to bash his skull in.
Packer said he then butchered Bell, ate as much as he could, packed away more meat, took Bell’s share of Swan’s money, and continued alone.
Packer said he threw away the remaining strips of Bell’s flesh because he hoped an animal would eat them.
General Adams called a conference of the five men and the agency officers to decide what to do next.
The five original party members said they did not believe a single part of Packer’s story.
The two Ute men said they knew of a place next to a lake that Packer had described, about 50 miles away across the hills.
A search party led by Herman Lauter and consisting of the five Utah miners, several agency officers, and Packer as guide was assembled at once.
After two weeks, near the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, Packer said he was lost and did not recognize the surroundings.
Nothing was found and the party returned to the agency.
On the way back, Packer tried to murder Herman Lauter with a knife.
Packer was caught, restrained, and arrested.
General Adams, who had been willing to believe Packer until then, concluded that Packer was dangerous after the attack on Lauter.
Packer was taken to Saguache and jailed outside town by the sheriff for his own protection.
Packer then said the men encountered a strong blizzard in the mountains.
Packer said heavy snow made them hopelessly lost and unable to retrace their route.
Packer said they also ran out of matches and had to carry hot embers in a steel coffee pot to light fires.
Packer said days passed with no game and ice fishing failed completely.
Packer said the men roasted and ate their shoes and tried to live on scant edible vegetation.
Packer said the men made a pact that if one died, his meat would save the others from starvation.
Packer said Israel Swan could go no further after days of hiking with almost no food.
Packer said they found a pine-shaded gulch next to a lake and made camp there.
Packer said Swan then died of hunger and exposure.
Packer signed a first confession saying Swan died first and was eaten by the other five persons about ten days out of camp.
Packer’s signed confession said Humphreys died four or five days later and was also eaten.
Packer’s signed confession said Humphreys had about $133 and that Packer found the pocketbook and took the money.
Packer’s signed confession said the butcher was later killed, apparently accidentally, while Packer was carrying wood and was also eaten.
Packer’s signed confession said Bell shot California with Swan’s gun and Packer killed Bell.
Packer’s signed confession said Packer shot Bell, covered up the remains, took a large piece along, and traveled 14 days to the agency.
In Packer’s later amended version, the men endured almost 20 days from Ouray’s camp and more than 10 days without substantial food.
In the amended version, James Humphrey died of exposure to extreme cold.
In the amended version, George Noon was killed days later by Shannon Bell solely for food.
In the amended version, Bell and Packer agreed to stand together until the end and not eat each other.
In the amended version, Bell later rushed at Packer with his rifle, intending to bludgeon him with the stock.
Packer said he took the valuables of the deceased because they no longer needed them, but he did not specify the items or the amount of money obtained.
While Packer was in jail, observers challenged his credibility.
Packer later said that only Bell and he remained after the other three men were dead.
The following August, John A. Randolph, an illustrator for Harper's Weekly, found the site of the incident.
Randolph discovered all five bodies at the foot of Slumgullion Pass, two miles southeast of Lake City, Colorado, in a pine-shaded gulch.
The bodies lay above the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, now colloquially known as Dead Man's Gulch.
The site matched the description of where Packer had originally claimed that only Bell was killed.
The snow covering the bodies and campsite had melted during the preceding four months.
Randolph sketched the scene and alerted authorities in nearby Lake City.
Harper's Weekly covered the story two months later in its October 17, 1874 edition and included Randolph's illustration.
The local coroner and law enforcement went to the site with about 20 volunteers and found all five bodies in various states of decomposition after four months outdoors.
First responders said it appeared that extreme violence had befallen the men.
Frank Miller's head was missing from the campsite.
Frank Miller's and Israel Swan's corpses had been heavily scavenged and were little more than scattered bones.
Israel's skull had a jagged chunk missing from it.
George Noon and James Humphrey were largely flayed torsos of rotting viscera attached to skeletal legs, but their faces remained intact and bearded.
Humphrey's face was slightly more decayed than Noon's.
Noon and Humphrey had head blows that suggested a hatchet and had noticeable broken bones.
Shannon Bell had skeletal legs, arms cut to the bones, hands that were still fully skinned, and a torso that was almost wholly flayed.
Bell's remaining corpse was a mass of viscera with a thick red beard and bushy hair still on his face.
The relatively undamaged state of Bell's face suggested that he had been the last to die.
The top of Bell's skull had been ripped open.
The three men whose bodies were still intact or partly intact had flesh and muscle cut from choice meaty locations.
No attempt had been made to consume bone marrow or any organs.
The condition of the bodies contradicted Packer's version of events.
The bodies were all together in one spot rather than scattered across miles.
Humphrey and Noon still had large portions of flesh, muscle, and organs that could have been eaten long before Bell allegedly tried to murder Packer.
The men had tattered cloths lashed to their rotting feet, replacing shoes they had probably eaten.
Moldy and tattered blankets lay beneath and beside the bodies.
A beaten path led from the corpses to a crude shelter used by Packer.
There was evidence that the deaths had occurred before supplies were totally exhausted.
Inside the shelter were possessions of the men that Packer had left behind.
The theory at the time was that Packer killed the men before supplies ran out to rob them, got snowed in, lived for months in his shelter, and walked to the bodies to cut off meat as needed.
Preston Nutter identified the bodies as the five missing men.
A rifle broken in two was found close to the bodies.
Because of damage to the remains, the rifle was presumed to have been used to bludgeon one or more of the men.
Officials buried the remains at the site, and the search party returned to Packer's makeshift jail to confront him, but he was missing.
Packer's jail was little more than a log cabin on ranch property belonging to the Saguache County Sheriff.
Months passed with no definitive evidence of a crime, no bodies discovered, and no formal charges against Packer other than the attempt on Lauter's life.
Saguache County authorities were reportedly unhappy about taxpayer money being spent to keep Packer under guard.
Packer was allegedly given a makeshift key for his irons and some supplies and escaped easily.
Nearly all of Saguache believed through rumor or deduction that Packer was guilty of robbery or murder.
Packer's life was constantly threatened by nearby townspeople.
Packer never said who helped him escape, how it happened, or why.
It was presumed that his guard had been bribed by Packer or by someone else.
The accepted theory at the time was that Packer had joined the party by overstating his qualifications as a mountain guide familiar with the area to accompany the men to Breckenridge.
That theory held that he at best led the party to miserable deaths through gross incompetence.
A more popular theory was that he left Ouray's camp with the five men with a premeditated plan to lead them into the wilderness and kill and rob them.
Nutter and Loutsenhizer tried to discredit Packer's claimed qualifications as a guide and highlighted his character flaws, inconsistent stories, and contradictions.
Local papers gave the case constant coverage with sensational headlines, negative comments about Packer's character, and imaginative theories that drew national and international attention.
Nearly all of Saguache and soon nearly the entire country and beyond believed Packer's responsibility for the deaths was beyond doubt.
Cannibalism was not seen as the main issue of Packer's guilt.
People then knew the Donner Party story and understood to some degree the need to eat in the wilderness.
Cannibalism was and is not illegal per se in the United States unless a murder is committed to obtain the flesh.
If someone murders to obtain flesh, the charge is murder, with the cannibalism treated as desecration or abuse of a corpse.
Packer claimed for the rest of his life that he was unjustly vilified and convicted for cannibalism rather than for murder, which he continued to deny.
On March 11, 1883, Jean "Frenchy" Cabazon found Packer in Cheyenne, Wyoming, living under the alias John Schwartze.
Cabazon had been a member of the original party that left Provo and had stayed in Chief Ouray's camp before reaching the destination later with Bob McGrue and Preston Nutter's party.
Cabazon encountered Packer when Packer approached him to buy supplies.
Cabazon reported Packer to the local sheriff, who apprehended him and contacted General Adams.
Cabazon was summoned to Cheyenne, confirmed Packer's identity, and accompanied him by train to Denver for Packer's second confession, which Packer signed on March 16.
Packer said he fled because he feared mob justice from the people of Saguache.
Because the actual crime was committed in Hinsdale County rather than Saguache County, Packer was sent to Lake City for detention and prosecution.
In Packer's second confession, he said Bell had killed the others after telling him to scout for a way out of the mountains and to find food.
Packer said he returned in the late evening after being gone most of the day.
Packer said Bell was roasting meat cut from Frank Miller's leg, with Miller's skull crushed by a hatchet and lying furthest from the fire down the stream.
Packer said the other three bodies were lying near the fire with hatchet cuts in the forehead.
Packer said he dropped his revolver in deep snow after shooting Bell and lost it.
Packer said he built a crude shelter from stray logs to fight the snow and wind and stayed away from the bodies.
Packer said another storm came and he sheltered for hours while starving.
Packer said he decided he had to eat something or die.
Packer said he returned to the fire, covered the men, took the piece of meat near the fire back to camp, cooked it, ate it, and lived off the flesh of the men for the bigger part of sixty days.
At the time of Packer's trial, Israel Swan's family reported that he had left for the expedition with about $6,000 in cash and gold and a valuable Winchester rifle.
Swan's money and rifle would have given a strong motive for murder, and Swan was 65 at the time of his death.
Packer was not found with any gold when arrested, and although he had some money left, it did not total in the thousands.
Packer's spending had been frivolous.
On April 6, a trial began in Lake City.
The prosecution argued that the only logical reason for Packer to travel through the mountains with so little food and supplies was to lead the men into the wilderness to kill and rob them.
Packer pleaded not guilty.
After seven days of testimony and examinations, he was found guilty of the premeditated murder of Israel Swan and sentenced to death by hanging on May 19, 1883.
It was presumed that Swan died on or around March 1.
The prosecution argued in court that Swan showed signs of a struggle at death and that the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep.
Otto Mears, Larry Dolan, Oliver D. Loutsenhizer, and Preston Nutter testified for the prosecution, with Nutter as the key witness.

Court records state that Judge M.B. Gerry sentenced Packer to be confined in Hinsdale County jail until May 19, 1883, then taken by the sheriff to an execution site in Lake City and hanged by the neck until dead.
Packer was spared the death penalty when his lawyers found that the 1874 murder statutes had been repealed and replaced with a savings clause.
In October 1885, the Colorado Supreme Court reversed the sentence on ex post facto grounds.
The court said the government could not sentence a man to death for a crime that occurred before Colorado became a state rather than a territory.
A second trial was held in Gunnison after a venue change granted by the Colorado Supreme Court and after a new Republican judge was appointed.
Packer and his counsel argued that Lake City's mainly Democratic community was too prejudiced for a fair trial.
Packer again pleaded not guilty.
The sentence amounted to 8 years per count, which was the maximum allowed per count.
At the time, the 40-year sentence was the longest custodial sentence in U.S. history.
Local hunters and officials said the winter of 1874 was severe but the San Juans where Packer's party camped still had abundant deer, antelope, and smaller game.
There was even a report that a deer carcass was found near the campsite.
That evidence weakened Packer's claim that wildlife was so scarce that the men quickly had to resort to cannibalism.
The choice to hike through the San Juan Mountains in midwinter, where snow could exceed six feet in one snowfall with blasting winds and freezing temperatures, was described as practically suicidal.
Locals had given Packer a safe route beside a main water source that could have provided fresh fish and kept them on course.
Instead, Packer chose a mountain path with minimal supplies because he believed it would be faster.
The route Packer and his companions took was nearly identical in length to the recommended route, though not in traverse, but far more dangerous.
Packer testified in his own defense at the second trial.
His account of the campsite events stayed relatively the same as his second official version.
Packer asked to be charged the 40 years only for Shannon Bell's death, the only killing he continued to claim.
The request was denied.
Packer filed appeals five times and was denied each time.
He sent letters to local newspapers saying he had been unjustly convicted by an unfair and unsympathetic judicial system and by ignorant small-minded people.
On June 19, 1899, the Colorado Supreme Court officially upheld Packer's sentence.
Packer was paroled on February 8, 1901, after a campaign led by an old acquaintance named Duane Hatch, who petitioned for nearly a decade before Polly Pry took notice.
Packer had served 18 years of his 40-year sentence.

Polly Pry of The Denver Post used Packer's Army service to portray him as a common man who was caught in a regrettable situation and who had been crucified for violating civilized sensibilities by resorting to cannibalism.
Pry's stories led to petitions and requests reaching Colorado Governor Charles Thomas's office, though they met strong opposition.
Thomas relented and, in his last official act before leaving office, paroled but did not pardon Packer on the condition that he would not try to profit from his story.
After parole, Packer worked as a guard at The Denver Post and later as a ranch hand.
Many believed The Denver Post job came directly from Pry and her employers securing his release.
Packer showed enduring respect for Pry and called her his Liberator.
His death was cited as "Dementia – trouble & worry," though his clinical cause of death has also been described as a stroke.
Packer was widely rumored to have become a vegetarian before death and was reported by acquaintances as a man rich with stories and liked by children.
He lived modestly and was reported to be charitable.
Packer was buried in Littleton, Colorado.
His grave has a veteran's tombstone listing his original regiment in 1862, replacing a marker that was stolen.
His first name is listed as Alfred, and he was known in life as both Alfred and Alferd.
He never succeeded in obtaining an official state pardon.
The Littleton Cemetery Association cemented over Packer's grave in 1973 to deter grave robbing and vandalism.
Edward Meyer of Ripley's Believe It or Not! Museum said the museum possessed Packer's dissected skull, which it bought from an anonymous party for $20,000.
No statement was made about how the museum verified the skull's authenticity, other than that the seller's information about its origin was sufficient.

If the skull belonged to Packer, his head was removed shortly before or after burial, dissected with the brain removed for study, preserved by an arsenic curing process, displayed by a traveling sideshow, sold to a private party, and later sold to Ripley's.
As of 2008, the skull was reported to be at the Ripley's Museum in San Antonio, Texas, after relocation from New Orleans following Hurricane Katrina.
On July 17, 1989, 115 years after Packer allegedly consumed his companions, James E. Starrs led an exhumation of the five bodies near the Lake Fork river upstream from Lake City.
The remains were found at the end of a residential driveway at a home belonging to a local surgeon and were buried only 13 inches below ground.
Starrs and Walter H. Birkby said they did not think cannibalism could ever be scientifically demonstrated because it would require a picture of the person actually eating human flesh.
Packer never denied cannibalism, so the investigation did not focus on that point.
The evidence was sufficient for Starrs to conclude that Packer had murdered his comrades.
Starrs believed Packer more likely murdered his companions for their belongings and resorted to cannibalism out of necessity rather than intent.
The remains were re-interred and given a proper burial with funeral rites.
Exhumation showed blunt force trauma to the skulls of two men, with no other notable disturbance except damage from butchering.
All skulls had damage to varying extents in their upper craniums, and fabric fibers were found in some skulls, suggesting their heads may have been covered with a blanket at death.
The three other skeletons showed defensive hacking marks across the radial and ulna bones of their forearms, including Shannon Bell's, consistent with shielding the face and body from an attack.
The skeletons showed no other noteworthy disturbance beyond damage made during butchering.
Shannon Bell was one of the skeletons with defensive forearm wounds.
These forearm wounds could have been sustained while shielding the face and body from an attack.
Packer claimed that Bell had murdered the others with hatchet blows to the head.
In his second version of the story, Packer never claimed that he had fought off Bell with a hatchet.
All five skeletons had numerous differing post-mortem injuries, including depressed fractures, butterfly fractures, butchering trauma, and hacking trauma.
The post-mortem injuries appear to contradict Packer's claim of minimal cannibalism.
Two skeletons other than Shannon Bell's were found to have cylindrical puncture wounds in the pelvic bone.
Some people have questioned whether all three pelvic marks were scavenging marks from a bear or possibly bullet wounds.
No definitive conclusion has been made about the pelvic puncture wounds.
One scenario suggested that two of the men were bludgeoned in their sleep by Packer.
In the same scenario, the three remaining men awoke and Packer shot them in the hips to incapacitate them if the punctures were bullet wounds.
The remaining men then may have tried to fight off Packer while he wielded a hatchet, and he killed them with blows to the head.
Packer then butchered the men and used their flesh to survive in his snowbound state and during his journey.
The different states of decomposition contradict that theory, although it is described as plausible.
It seems unlikely that Packer shot three of the five men in the hip unless he was trying to debilitate them before killing them.
Further analysis of entry and exit geometry could clarify the initial cause, but no such examination has been done to date.
Packer's ultimate motivation for the murders has been heavily debated and has several possible theories.
In 1994, David P. Bailey, curator of history at the Museum of Western Colorado, began an investigation to find more conclusive results than Starrs regarding Packer's claim of having shot Bell.
In the Audrey Thrailkill collection of firearms at the museum was a Colt revolver reportedly found at the site of Packer's alleged crime.
Exhaustive investigation into the pistol's background uncovered trial-era documents.
A Civil War veteran who visited the crime scene said Shannon Bell had been shot twice and the other victims had been killed with a hatchet.
The veteran said that, after studying Bell, he noticed a severe bullet wound to the pelvic area and a bullet hole through Bell's wallet.
This evidence seemed to corroborate Packer's claim that Bell had killed the other victims and that Packer shot Bell in self-defense.
By 2000, Bailey had not yet proven a link between the antique pistol and Alfred Packer.
In 2001, Dr. Richard Dujay at Mesa State College analyzed archived forensic samples from the 1989 exhumation with an electron microscope.
Dujay found microscopic lead fragments in soil taken from under Shannon Bell's remains.
Spectrograph analysis matched those lead fragments to the bullets remaining in Packer's pistol.
It now appears certain that at least Bell was shot.
Whether Bell was shot in self-defense remains unanswered.
In Dashiell Hammett's novel The Thin Man, Nick Charles advises Gilbert Wynant to read a selection about Packer's expeditions.
The selection in The Thin Man comes from Thomas Samuel Duke's Celebrated Criminal Cases of America.
Thomas Samuel Duke gave Packer's first name as Alfred in that selection.
Harold Schechter wrote the true-crime book Man-Eater about Packer.
In 1968, students at the University of Colorado Boulder named their new cafeteria grill the Alferd G. Packer Memorial Grill.
The cafeteria grill's slogan was 'Have a friend for lunch!'
Customers at the grill can order an El Canibal beefburger.
A giant map outlining Packer's travels through Colorado was displayed on the wall of the grill.
The grill has since been renamed the Alferd Packer Restaurant & Grill.
In 1977, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Bob Bergland tried to terminate a contract for the USDA cafeteria food service but was blocked by the General Services Administration.
To embarrass the GSA, Bergland and his employees held a press conference on August 10, 1977, to unveil a plaque naming the executive cafeteria The Alferd Packer Memorial Grill.
At the press conference, Bergland said Packer's life exemplified the spirit and fare of the cafeteria and would 'serve all mankind'.
Barbara Walters covered the event on ABC Evening News.
The stratagem succeeded and the contracts were terminated soon afterward.
Bergland removed the plaque after accepting the bureaucratic objection that it lacked official GSA authorization.
The plaque is now displayed on the wall of the National Press Club's The Reliable Source members-only bar.
The plaque also serves as a memorial to Stanley Weston, a USDA employee who lived from 1931 to 1984.
The National Press Club's hamburger is called the Alfred Packer Burger.
The comedy musical Cannibal! The Musical was released exclusively to Boulder, Colorado, in 1993 and released in the rest of the United States in 1996.
Cannibal! The Musical was Trey Parker's directorial debut.
Phil Ochs wrote 'The Ballad of Alferd Packer' in 1964 about the expedition and its aftermath.
Ochs used humor in the song, matching the lighthearted ongoing attitude toward Packer and his alleged crimes.
The song never appeared on any of Ochs's studio or live albums.
The song later appeared on several compilations released after Ochs's death in 1976, including the 2010 On My Way compilation of demos from 1963.
C. W. McCall wrote the song 'Comin' Back for More' about Packer.

skim_summary: Alferd Packer gave multiple evolving confessions regarding the deaths and cannibalism of his expedition companions.
Packer's legal trajectory involved initial sentencing, a overturned death sentence by the Colorado Supreme Court, resentencing to 40 years, and eventual parole.
Public officials and political figures treated Packer's case with a mix of severe legal judgment and humorous or pun-filled rhetoric.
Packer persists as a popular cultural figure with named establishments and annual commemorative traditions across multiple states.

There’s a lot of information still circulating about Alferd Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal and dubbed by local papers as the “Man-Eater.”
In the fall of 1873, Packer left with 20 prospectors on an expedition toward San Juan country. Many of the men returned home from the expedition after fierce snowstorms boxed in the party but six men including Packer continued on. Only Packer returned in the winter of 1874.
The Arrow reported in January 1965 that a blizzard caught the six men without sufficient food and Packer wandered into the Los Pinos Agency in Southwest Colorado three months later. “After a confession, a search for the bodies and a trial, Packer was sentenced to forty years at the Colorado State Penitentiary,” the article states.
Packer gave three confessions — one in May 1874, one in March 1883 and a final confession was sent in a letter to the Rocky Mountain News in August 1897. In the first confession, Packer detailed the ill-fated voyage with minimal information, noting the first two deaths were circumstantial given the rough conditions and that everyone partook in cannibalism to stay alive. He said one man was “killed accidentally” while he was collecting firewood and that another man in the party, Shannon Bell, killed a man he called “California” and said he then killed Bell in self-defense before traveling for 14 days back to civilization.
In his second confession, Packer said he was asked by the party to go up a nearby hill to see if he could see anything farther away that would help them navigate. When he returned to camp after a full day of going up and coming back down the hillside, Packer said that Bell had killed the entire camp and was eating the leg of a man that he had roasted in the campfire. When he approached the fire, Packer said Bell rushed at him and Packer shot him through the stomach with the rifle he’d taken on his trip up the hillside. “I went back to the fire covered the men up and fetched to the camp the piece of meat that was near the fire,” Packer said in his 1883 confession. “I made a new fire near my camp and cooked the piece of meat and ate it. I tried to get away every day but could not so I lived off the flesh of these men, the bigger part of the 60 days I was out.” Packer’s third confession included more details but had largely the same information.
District Court Judge Melville Gerry during sentencing in 1883 reportedly said, “stand up, Alferd Packer, you voracious, man-eating s– of a b—-. There were seven Democrats in Hinsdale County, and you ate five of them. I sentence you to hang until you are dead, dead, dead as a warning against reducing the Democratic population of the state,” the Washington Post reported in April 1984.
Packer’s death sentence was overturned by the Colorado Supreme Court in 1885 because of a “grandfather clause.” Packer’s attorney assigned several errors to the court including that Packer didn’t get a speedy trial and his indictments on the murder charges came after what was then a statute of limitations consisting of three years. Packer was resentenced in 1886 to 40 years in prison and was paroled by former Gov. Charles Thomas in 1901.
The United Press International in 1982 reported that Packer’s posthumous pardon was declined by then-Gov. Richard Lamm the year before. In a pun-filled speech, Lamm said, “I realize that several of you have a bone to pick with me because of my refusal to grant Alferd Packer an unconditional pardon last year.” Lamm told the onlookers in 1982 at a bust unveiling of Packer at the Capitol Rotunda, “you claim that the evidence indicates that Mr. Packer killed but one man, and that one only in self-defense. Unfortunately, the proof was in the pudding and Alferd ate that, too.”
The New York Times reported in 1982 that Lamm congratulated sculptor Tom Miller at Packer’s bust unveiling, saying, “in the immortal words of Alferd Packer, uttered when asked how he liked his fellow man, I say [to] you, Tom Miller, ‘Well done!’”
Packer remains a wildly popular figure in state history. A restaurant in Boulder, Colorado, the Alferd Packer Grill, was named in his honor. Events and traditions honoring Packer take place annually in Colorado and 12 other states, according to the Washington Post.

sources.title: Alferd Packer: The Truth is Out There (Or Right Here)
sources.creator: history.denverlibrary.org
skim_summary: Alferd Packer's survival of a 1874 winter expedition resulted in murder charges, jail escape, eventual imprisonment, and eventual release.
Popular folklore surrounding Packer, such as exaggerated judicial quotes, conflicts with historical archival records.
Public perception of Packer ranges from dark western folklore to factual historical re-evaluation.
sources.full_text:
The story of Alferd Packer, "The Colorado Cannibal," is one of the most notorious - and most misunderstood - tales from the pages of Colorful Colorado's history.
Packer, as you might know, was a prospector who set out for Colorado's gold fields with a party of five other men across the rugged San Juan Mountains during the winter of 1874. Packer was the only man who would survive that ill-fated trip with his life. His reputation (as evidenced by the fact that we're writing about him today) did not survive.
The soon-to-be-notorious Packer aroused suspicion when he emerged from the woods with a pocket full of cash and no traveling party. After being accused of murdering the other men, Packer told the story that would define the rest of his life and earn him a permanent place in Colorado history.
According to Packer, the members of his party died one at a time and were consumed by the other members until it came down to just him and one other member, Shannon Bell. In Packer's story, a desperately hungry Bell attempted to beat the Grim Reaper by killing the Colorado Cannibal before he died of natural causes. Bell was killed in the ensuing fight and Packer was left with no choice but to eat the man who would have eaten him.
Not surprisingly, local authorities weren't convinced by Packer's story and he was eventually charged with murder. Packer promptly escaped from the Saguache jail and stayed on the lam for eight years before authorities tracked him down. He was eventually found guilty of Bell's murder in 1883. He was originally sentenced to death, but after a second trial in 1885 he received a 40-year sentence, of which he served 16 years before being released and living out his life in relative peace.
Though Packer himself died peacefully, his legacy has been anything but settled, and his story has been the subject of historical and popular discussion ever since.
Alferd Packer: Fact vs. Fiction
The story we know about Alferd Packer and the story that actually occurred are not always the same story. Fortunately, the real story of Packer's crimes, trials and life can be found right here at the Western History/Genealogy Department.
Take, for example, Judge M.B. Gerry's famous quote that was supposedly uttered while handing down the sentence in Packer's first trial:
Stand up yah voracious man-eatin' sonofabitch and receive yir sintince. When yah came to Hinsdale County, there was siven Dimmycrats. But you, yah et five of 'em, goddam yah. I sintince yah t' be hanged by th' neck ontil yer dead, dead, dead, as a warnin' in reducin' th' Dimmycratic populayshun of this county. Packer, you Republican cannibal, I would sintince ya ta hell but the statutes forbid it.
As it turns out, Judge Gerry, like most Colorado residents, didn't talk like Yosemite Sam, which Fred M. Mazzula points out in his book, Al Packer, A Colorado Cannibal. Mazzula used transcripts from the trial to discover that what Judge Gerry actually said was:
Alfred Packer, the judgment of this court is that you be removed from hence to the jail of Hinsdale County and there confined until the 19th day of May, A.D. 1883, and that on said 19th day of May, 1883, you be taken from thence by the sheriff of Hinsdale County to a place of execution prepared for this purpose, at some point within the corporate limits of the town of Lake City, in the said country of Hinsdale, and between the hours of 10 A.M. and 3 P.M. of said day, you, then and there, by said sheriff, be hung by the neck until you are dead, dead, dead, and my God have mercy upon your soul.
While Gerry's real quote is less colorful, it does have the benefit of being accurate.
Finding the Truth for Yourself
Researchers and history buffs who want to learn more about Packer's life and crimes can find an array of materials at Denver Public Library that can be used to prove, or disprove, various pieces of the Packer legend.
Besides microfilm of Denver and Colorado newspapers of the era (including a complete run of the Denver Post and Rocky Mountain News), WH/G visitors can access a number of Packer books, including books like The Alfred G. Packer Victims Exhumation Project Lake City, Colorado, July 17, 1989 that utilizes archeology to get to the truth of what really happened during that ill-fated journey. Of course, we also have a few unique items (we wouldn't be a special collection if we didn't!) including copies of Packer's confession and an unused warrant for his execution...which obviously never happened.
Finally
Packer's story involves a whole lot more than a starving man who was reduced to consuming human flesh in an effort to survive a high country winter. Indeed, Packer was a Civil War veteran who spent nearly a decade on the run from justice and, ultimately, found some redemption from the people of Colorado, or at least from the justice system.
And while Packer's story has long been the subject of gallows humor and amusements, such as Alferd Packer's High Protein Gourmet Cookbook, there's really nothing funny about the tale at all. In the end, five men died agonizing deaths in the cruel mountain cold, while a sixth had his own life irrevocably altered.
But if you're looking to find out the real story behind the story you think you know, the truth is out there.

sources.title: Alfred Packer ate 'em, forensic expert says - UPI Archives
sources.creator: KAREN TIMMONS
skim_summary: A modern forensic exhumation project concluded that Alfred Packer murdered and defleshed his five fellow prospectors in 1874.
The historical record surrounding Alfred Packer features conflicting narratives, legal reversals, and persistent legends.
sources.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- More than a century after Alfred Packer was first accused of killing -- and then dining on -- five fellow prospectors in Colorado, a forensic law professor said Friday he has proven that Packer was 'guilty as sin.'
Packer 'butchered his five fellow prospectors to death and then skinned them for all their bones were worth as he feasted and feted on their flesh,' said James Starrs, professor of law and forensic science at George Washington University.
Starrs, leader of a team of forensic investigators who exhumed the bodies of the five victims from a mass grave in the San Juan mountains last July, said, 'The added scientific evidence, in my opinion, convicts him (Packer) beyond any shadow of a doubt.'
Packer was one of six prospectors who, flush with gold fever, ignored the dangers of winter and headed into the Colorado mountains in February 1874.
A scurrilous liar and thief by reputation, Packer has been the source of legend since the day in April 1874 that he wandered out of the mountains alone.
He claimed his five companions had all died or been killed during the harsh winter and that the survivors had eaten the flesh of the dead, one by one, to avoid starvation.
Later that summer the remains of the five were discovered together and Packer's many stories of the adventure began to unravel. In 1883 he was charged with murdering all five. In one confession, he admitted to shooting one man -- in self-defense.
According to legend, the Lake City, Colo., judge who sentenced Packer to death accused him of eating five of the seven Democrats in the county, but historians say that account is apocryphal.
Packer won an appeal on a technicality, was retried and convicted on involuntary manslaughter charges. He was paroled in 1901, after a Denver Post columnist crusaded on his behalf.
'Over the years since 1874, Packer has been lionized, apologized and sympathized,' Starrs said, noting attempts to have him pardoned posthumously.
Displaying a T-shirt bearing five skulls and crossed bones and the legend 'Gimme Five! The Packer Project,' Starrs told reporters gathered to hear the expedition's findings, 'Alfred Packer was as guilty as sin and his sins were all mortal.'
Starrs said the team's examination of the bones of the victims showed that none had been shot and four had been killed by hatchet blows to the head. The fifth skull has not been found.
The bones of all five also revealed, he said, numerous knife marks indicating 'defleshing.'
Citing 'unmistakeable proof of cannibalism,' Starrs said Packer used the 'natural refrigerator' of the Colorado winter to preserve his victims and dined on them until spring.
'He was having human flesh filets morning, noon and night,' Starrs said.
The professor said, based on Packer's reputation, he believes the prospector's motive in the murders was initially to steal his companions' belongings and that he then turned to cannibalism.
Starrs said his aim in the project was not only to settle the debate over Packer's guilt, but also to 'put forensic science on parade.'
The exhumation project, which cost an estimated $10,000 to $15,000, utilized a variety of modern forensic science techniques, including ground penetrating radar and laboratory inspection of the remains.
One issue the scientific team did not settle was the spelling of Packer's first name -- Starrs used 'Alfred,' as do official court papers from the time. But Packer signed his name 'Alferd.'
Regardless, when Packer died in 1907 in Jefferson County, Colo., the official cause of death listed simply: 'Senility -- trouble and worry.'

sources.title: Was the ‘Colorado Cannibal’ a villain or a victim? You decide.
sources.creator: Brendan Bures; Benjamin Rasmussen
skim_summary: Forensic exhumations and scientific investigations into the 1874 deaths yielded conflicting conclusions among experts.
Packer maintained that he acted in self-defense after Shannon Wilson Bell killed the other prospectors.
Local public opinion and social stigma, partly tied to Packer's epilepsy and odd behavior, heavily influenced perceptions of his guilt.
sources.full_text:
Was the ‘Colorado Cannibal’ a villain or a victim? You decide.
Alferd Packer survived for weeks in the frozen wilderness by eating his companions—this much he admitted. But details uncovered decades later don’t match the official narrative.
July 17, 1989 was hot and muggy in Lake City, Colorado, and sweat dripped from the grad students’ faces as they dug up the skeletons. When they exposed the first skull, a gaping hole in its forehead, the crowd of onlookers let out a gasp and reporters rushed to the town’s four public pay phones to file the sensational story: “Professor Exhumes 100-Year-Old Victims of Colorado Cannibal.”
When the team led by law professor James Starrs finished digging, they had unearthed the skeletons of five men. All were allegedly murdered and partially consumed by a shifty character known variously as Alferd Packer, Alfred Packer, and, most notoriously, the Colorado Cannibal.
There are several versions of Packer’s story, but the essential facts are these: Born near Pittsburgh in 1842, he suffered from epilepsy from an early age—an affliction and stigma that would dog his steps all his days. He enlisted in the Union Army during the Civil War but was discharged due to his frequent seizures.
After the war Packer rattled around the country, landing in Utah in 1873. Late that fall he joined a group 20 prospectors headed to southwestern Colorado. There was news of a gold strike there, and “marvelous tales of enormous fortunes to be had for the mere asking,” according to one newspaper account.
Travel was slow going, especially when winter arrived early and with a vengeance. By late January the prospectors had run out of provisions and were eating livestock feed when they arrived at a Ute Indian encampment. The leader, Chief Ouray, gave the men food and shelter and urged them to stay the winter, warning that no Ute would travel under such severe conditions.
Most of the group prudently accepted the chief’s offer, but six prospectors in the grip of gold fever—Israel Swan, George Noon, Frank Miller, James Humphrey, Shannon Wilson Bell, and Packer—decided to forge ahead. They soon lost their way in the rugged San Juan Mountains and became snowbound.
In mid-April, only one of the six men emerged from the mountains alive. It was Packer, looking suspiciously well fed and flush with cash. He spent over $100 on booze and gambling and seemed strangely uninterested in food.
When questioned about the fate of his traveling companions, Packer was evasive. Finally, under interrogation, he gave the first of multiple contradictory confessions.
“We ate old man Swann first,” he began. The strong ate the weak one by one, leaving their bodies miles apart, until only he and Bell remained. Bell then tried to kill him, Packer claimed, so he shot him dead.
Packer was arrested on murder charges but escaped before going to trial. Meanwhile, a traveling illustrator for Harper’s Weekly made a grisly discovery: the decomposing remains of the five missing prospectors. Four had fractured skulls, one was headless, and all bore signs of butchering. The men had died together in one place, refuting Packer’s confession.
Nine years later, the fugitive Packer was captured in Wyoming and returned to Lake City, where he was tried for murder, found guilty, and sentenced to die by hanging. But the verdict was overturned on a technicality and the confessed cannibal was spared the noose.
Packer was tried a second time, convicted on the lesser charge of manslaughter, and sentenced to 40 years in the state penitentiary. He proved a model prisoner and was granted parole after serving just 15 years.
Decades later, in 1989, Starrs concluded his investigation by pronouncing Packer “guilty as sin.” Case closed.
Or was it? Not everyone who examined the evidence was so cocksure. The late Walter Birkby, a University of Arizona forensic anthropologist who assisted Starrs, stated: "We found nothing to corroborate or refute anything Packer said. We'll never know who did it based on any solid physical evidence.”
If Birkby was agnostic, Michelle Pierce, Lake City’s former town clerk, is convinced Packer did not murder the five men. Her archival research turned up many details that don’t square with the official narrative. And it paints a portrait not of a calculating killer, but of a pitiable soul whose social pathologies stemmed from a misunderstood disease and the harsh judgments of his contemporaries.
“People really disliked him,” Pierce says, “probably in large part because they were afraid of him.”
In the course of time, fear of Packer would be replaced by a kind of dubious fame. Today he is at once the patron saint of Lake City and its antihero, its most celebrated son and, as one newspaperman quipped, its “disreputable relative who keeps reappearing at inopportune moments.”
For a short spell in the 1870s, prospectors flooded into Lake City. But the boom was brief, and nowadays the remote mountain town, elevation 8,661 feet, is home to a few hundred residents. Most visitors come to this wild corner of the Colorado Rockies to hunt, fish, or hike. Some come hoping to catch a glimpse of Al Packer’s ghost.
Cannibal Grill and coffin races
I drive up to Lake City hoping to sift fact from folklore. Strolling the town’s wood-plank sidewalks, I see no signs of ambivalence about Packer—but plenty of unabashed boosterism. Here you can eat at the Packer Saloon & Cannibal Grill and stay at the Cannibal Cabins. Over the years the town has hosted an annual Al Packer Day featuring coffin races, mystery-meat eating competitions, and an Al Packer look-alike contest.
When I ask old-timers around town for information about Packer, almost everyone points me to Grant Houston, head of the Hinsdale County Historical Society and editor and publisher of the local newspaper, the Lake City Silver World.
“Many people here, myself included, would tell you that Packer was guilty,” Houston says when we chat in his office. “I grew up with the people who had been here at the turn of the century, and their grandparents who had been here, perhaps on the Packer jury even. They believed Packer lured the men up here, because they had money or guns or something he coveted, dispatched them, and then took off.”
While Houston sides with the Packer jury, others have raised doubts about the jurors’ qualifications. Of 57 prospective jurors interviewed, 54 admitted prior knowledge of the case, and 44 stated they had preconceived opinions of Packer’s guilt. Eventually, Judge Melville Gerry had to order the sheriff to “scour the highways and byways” for candidates to fill the jury. He somehow accomplished the job in a few hours.
'Dead, dead, dead'
The Hinsdale County Courthouse in Lake City, built in 1877 and recently restored to its historic appearance, is the oldest operating courthouse in Colorado. As I walk through the two-story structure, the wood floors creak and groan under every step. The walls are lined with Packer memorabilia, including newspaper accounts and official records from the trial.
The second-floor courtroom looks much as it did in Packer’s day—minus the porcelain spittoons and signs ordering “Do Not Spit on the Floor.” A portrait of Packer hangs in a back corner.
On April 9, 1883, the day Packer’s trial began, the courtroom was filled to capacity. The prosecution presented some two dozen witnesses. Otto Mears, a prominent local businessman, testified that Packer possessed valuable Wells Fargo drafts when he emerged from the mountains. Constable Herman Lauter recounted how Packer, when ordered to hand over a knife, instead lunged at him with murder in his eyes.
Preston Nutter, one of the prospectors who waited out the winter with the Ute Indians, testified that Packer had been skulking about trying to discover how much money each man was carrying.
When Packer took the stand, he gave a rambling, long-winded testimony lasting over six hours. According to his telling of events, the fierce weather forced him and the other prospectors to make camp in a ravine that offered some shelter from the snow and wind.
“We ate our goatskin moccasins and subsisted on rosebuds until we were weakened and emaciated and mentally completely distracted,” Packer later wrote in a letter. “Yet if there was any one sane of the six, I was the one.”
One day as the freezing men huddled under their blankets, Packer left camp to look for a way out of the mountains. When he returned, he found Shannon Wilson Bell roasting meat over a fire. As Packer approached, Bell grabbed a hatchet and came after him.
Packer lifted his gun and shot his assailant, then seized the hatchet and finished him off with a blow to the head. To his horror, he discovered that Bell had hacked the other men to death.
Packer freely admitted that he survived on the men’s flesh until he was able to escape the mountains, but he adamantly maintained that he killed only Bell, and that in self-defense.
The jury didn’t buy his story—not only due to the damning testimony of the prosecution’s witnesses, but also because of Packer’s odd performance on the stand. He habitually referred to himself in the third person—as in, “Packer was as much thought of as any man”—and often seemed more interested in settling personal vendettas than proving his innocence. Decrying Constable Lauter as a liar, Packer blustered: “To think that one little Dutchman could take a knife away from me. No, sir!”
The jury wasted little time in finding Packer guilty of murder, and Judge Gerry sentenced him to be “hung from your neck until you are dead, dead, dead.”
Before Packer went to the gallows, however, Colorado’s Supreme Court overturned his death sentence. The alleged crime had occurred before Colorado achieved statehood, and an old territorial statute banning the death penalty took precedence.
Lake City old-timers were outraged and threatened to hang the maneater themselves, so Packer’s second trial was moved to Gunnison, some 50 miles away. There Packer was found guilty on the lesser charge of manslaughter and sentenced to 40 years in prison.
The smoking gun?
In 1994, more than a century after Packer was marched off to prison, David Bailey, former curator of history at the Museums of Western Colorado, was inventorying a collection of historic firearms when he came across an 1862 Colt revolver, a sidearm commonly used by 19th-century prospectors. Three .38 caliber cartridges were still loaded in the pistol. The yellowed accession card stated: “This gun found at the site where Alferd Packer killed and ate his companions.”
The discovery launched Bailey on a 10-year investigation. He learned that during the 1989 exhumation, a hole about the size of a thimble had been found in Bell’s hip bone. Professor Starrs attributed the hole to a scavenging animal’s fangs, but Bailey wondered if it might have been made by a bullet.
He persuaded the Hinsdale County Historical Society, which still owned the 1989 forensic samples, to share them with Richard Dujay, director of the Electron Microscopy Lab at Mesa State College. Dujay and his team examined Bell’s samples and discovered a tiny fragment of lead. The fragment’s chemical composition matched that of the bullets in Bailey’s old Colt revolver.
Using a similar 1860s pistol, the team fired a bullet into an elk hip bone. The resulting hole matched the one in Bell’s hip, supporting Packer’s claim that he shot Bell. Bailey believed he had cracked the case.
Grant Houston, however, remains skeptical. Back in the day, he says, tourists were always finding old guns and bullets near the massacre site and claiming they belonged to Packer or one of the other prospectors. Even Michelle Pierce, Packer’s staunchest defender, is unconvinced that Bailey’s pistol is the smoking gun.
But in the court of public opinion, Bailey consistently wins his case. Through the years, residents of Lake City, Boulder, and other Colorado towns held mock trials for Packer. Actors played the key roles and audience members served as jurors. When Bailey’s evidence was included, the jurors acquitted Packer more often than not.
“Even though they were mock trials,” Bailey says, “it was kind of vindicating to me.”
“Blind injustice”
Seeking vindication became the goal of Packer’s life after he landed in prison. He made many appeals for a pardon but was refused time and again.
In 1899, Denver Post writer Polly Pry visited Packer at the Colorado State Penitentiary in Canon City. “The corroding desire for freedom has eaten into his heart,” she reported, “and the blind injustice of the world has seared into his soul.”
Believing Packer had been unjustly tried and convicted, Pry launched a media campaign to bring attention to his plight. Packer gained many allies who signed a petition calling for his pardon.
“Supposing the man did commit the crime,” one supporter wrote to Colorado Governor Charles Thomas. “After such privations, I do not see how he could be held responsible. The line between sanity and insanity is often very thin, and I don’t think we understand it.”
As his last act in office, Governor Thomas granted Packer parole, but not pardon.
Packer took up residence in Denver but found city life intolerable, so he moved a few miles out to Littleton to be closer to the mountains. He bought some copper claims and went about prospecting again, until his epilepsy got the better of him. He died in 1907, age 65.
The day I visit Packer’s grave in Littleton, purple clouds swirl above the mountains to the west. Previous visitors have left offerings at the foot of his grave: a toy firetruck, a marijuana vape pen, a vase for flowers now gone. A wooden bench invites visitors to sit and reflect, so I do.
Today Packer is regarded mostly as a meme and a punchline. At the University of Colorado Boulder, about 40 miles from where I sit, students can eat at the Alferd Packer Grill, where they’re greeted by a giant portrait of the cannibal and the slogan “Have a friend for lunch!”
Like Lake City’s boosters, UC-Boulder students have hosted Al Packer Days wearing tee shirts with phrases like “Finger lickin' good” and “When you care enough to eat the very best.”
Sitting at Packer's grave, I wonder how many people know how he actually felt about eating human flesh. “Can you imagine my situation?” he wrote in one of many letters he penned insisting on his innocence and seeking a pardon. “My comrades dead and I left alone surrounded by the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation? My body weak, my mind acted upon in such an awful manner that the greatest wonder is that I ever returned to a rational condition.”
I sit staring at Packer’s tombstone until something wet hits my face. The cemetery’s lawn sprinklers are spraying directly on the Packer memorial bench. I take it as yet another joke on the Colorado Cannibal, only this time I can’t help but laugh.
Finally, I rise and bid Packer goodbye. Then I get into my car and drive west on the interstate until the mountains swallow me whole.

Leonel Campbell Ross O'Bryan (1857–16 July 1938), known under the pen name Polly Pry, was a controversial reporter for The Denver Post and later as a freelancer in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. She is best known for her connection to the case of Alfred Packer as an investigative reporter.[1][2]
Early life
[edit]Pry was born to a wealthy family in 1857. Aged fifteen, she eloped to Mexico with a railroad industrialist named George Anthony. Five years later, Pry left Anthony and moved to New York to become a reporter.[3] While initially being rejected by The New York Times, she succeeded in getting a trial assignment on a recent slum fire. The article she then produced was good enough to earn her a full time job there.[4]
In 1898, Pry was hired by Frederick Bonfils for the Denver Post, becoming the paper's first female reporter. She was a member of the Denver Woman's Press Club.[5]
Relationship with Packer
[edit]Pry met Alfred Packer in 1901 while she was writing an article on the prison where he was incarcerated. She advocated for him in print throughout the trial, helping to win his release.
After the trial, she was present during a confrontation between the attorney for Packer, and the owners of the Post, who had hired him. The owners learned that the attorney had taken a double payment, and demanded he return the money. During the confrontation, the attorney, W. W. Anderson, pulled a gun and shot both of the men; as he prepared to shoot again she jumped in front of Harry Heye Tammen, trying to shield him. Anderson threatened to shoot her if she didn't move. However, she stalled him long enough for the police to arrive and used her skirt to stop the bleeding. Later, rumors began circulating that her skirts saved her publishers' lives by slowing down bullets from the gun.[1]
Later life
[edit]When union workers boycotted The Denver Post for her stance on labor issues and immigration, she founded her own paper, Polly Pry. This brought further attacks from gunmen on her, this time in her home rather than her workplace.[6]
She was a strong advocate of free speech and came to the aid of French war orphans during World War I.
Pry died on 16 July 1938, aged eighty.
In popular culture
[edit]Two film versions of the Alferd Packer story have included Polly Pry. In Jim Roberson's The Legend of Alfred Packer (1980), she was portrayed by Cynthia Nessin. The incident with Anderson (who was not named, and called "Gunman" in the credits) was included, but after she begins telling Packer's story, she does not appear again in the film, involved or otherwise, and the shooting is not mentioned again. She is depicted as a hard-drinking and forceful person. Trey Parker's Cannibal! The Musical featured Toddy Walters in the role, which went more deeply into her involvement with the case but ignored the fact that she was married in order to make her a love interest for Packer.[7][8]

Alferd Packer
The infamous prospect party led by Alferd Packer entered the San Juan region in winter of 1873 - 1874. Led by Packer, the party of 21 prospectors departed from Bingham Canyon, Utah on November 8, 1873 in hopes of being among the first to locate mining claims in the San Juan region.
They reached the Ute encampment near present-day Montrose on January 21, 1874 with their food and supplies exhausted. Here, the party of 21 prospectors split into three factions. Chief Ouray warned the men about the treacherous winter conditions ahead of them.
Some men paid a trespassing fee to Chief Ouray and camped with the Utes for the rest of the winter; others accepted a week's worth of provisions from Ouray and traveled on to the Los Pinos Agency in Saguache County (this group nearly perished after losing its way in the harsh mountain wilderness).
A third group ignored Ouray's warnings. Five prospectors outfitted with a week's worth of provisions followed Packer on February 9 southeast then south along the Lake Fork past the site that would become the townsite of Lake City within six months.
Nothing was heard from the six prospectors for nearly three months until Packer arrived alone on April 16 at the Los Pinos Agency. He proceeded on to Saguache, were he attracted suspicion by spending large sums of money and having in his possession a rifle that had belonged to one of the missing men. Packer was arrested and jailed at Saguache and issued a confession to the crime.
In August of that year, a prospecting party discovered the bodies of the five missing men. An illustrator from Harpers Weekly accompanied the group and recorded the scene in visual graphic detail that riveted national attention on the grisly crime.
Packer escaped the jail in Saguache and remained a free man for nine years. He was finally apprehended in Wyoming in 1883 and brought back to Hinsdale County where he was tried, found guilty of murder, and sentenced to hang.
Packer appealed for a re-trial on the grounds that the crime was committed on the Ute Reservation in early 1874 and should therefore be subject to federal rather than local jurisdiction. He was incarcerated at Gunnison where he awaited retrial for nearly four years, in the meantime becoming a local celebrity. Packer's retrial in 1886 found him guilty of five counts of manslaughter and he was sentenced to forty years of hard labor at the state penitentiary in Cañon City.
In the early 1900s, news reporter Polly Pry launched a journalistic campaign to release Packer, and Denver Post publishers Fred Bonfils and Harry Tammen hired a lawyer to defend him. Packer received parole in 1905 and died two years later at a ranch near Deer Creek in western Jefferson County.
Packer's case reflects the eagerness of prospectors to trespass into the Ute reservation and illustrates how swiftly development took place once the San Juan region opened.
The incident is also significant as the only known trial in the United States associated with human cannibalism, attracting national and international attention to Lake City and its environs. Although modern myth states that Packer was convicted of cannibalism, this is totally incorrect.
